measure: median earnings for each $100 that men earn
statement: In 2025, women earned 84 cents for every dollar men earned.
source_title: U.S. Census Bureau, "Income in the United States: 2025" (P60-289)
notes: Female-to-male earnings ratio, Table 12. It was 80.6% in 2024. It compares medians and does not control for job or hours beyond full-time.

measure: gender classification error rate, IBM classifier
statement: IBM's face analysis tool got the gender of darker-skinned women wrong about 1 in 3 times, and of lighter-skinned men almost never.
source_title: Buolamwini, Joy, and Timnit Gebru, "Gender Shades: Intersectional Accuracy Disparities in Commercial Gender Classification"
notes: IBM classifier, Table 4 (p. 9). Microsoft and Face++ showed the same pattern (20.8% vs 0.0%, 34.5% vs 0.8%). Year = publication year. "Darker" = Fitzpatrick skin types IV–VI, so it also includes some of our mid skin tones. This tests gender classification, not face recognition.

measure: average word error rate of 5 speech recognition systems
statement: Speech recognition systems made 1.8× as many errors for Black speakers as for white speakers.
source_title: Koenecke, Allison, et al., "Racial Disparities in Automated Speech Recognition," PNAS
notes: 42 white and 73 Black speakers, matched on age and gender. Year = publication year; the systems were tested in 2019.

measure: callback rate for job applications (identical résumés)
statement: Résumés with Black-sounding names got 33% fewer callbacks than the same résumés with white-sounding names.
source_title: Bertrand, Marianne, and Sendhil Mullainathan, "Are Emily and Greg More Employable than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination," NBER Working Paper 9873
notes: Field experiment, about 5,000 résumés to job ads in Boston and Chicago, 2001–2002. Table 1, all sent résumés. The published version (American Economic Review, 2004) reports 9.65% vs 6.45%.

measure: maternal deaths per 100,000 live births
statement: In 2024, Black women died of maternal causes 3.2× as often as white women.
source_title: Hoyert, Donna L., "Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2024," NCHS Health E-Stats
notes: Maternal death = during pregnancy or within 42 days after it. Hispanic women: 12.1, Asian women: 18.1. The rate for Black women was 69.9 in 2021.

measure: maternal deaths per 100,000 live births
statement: In 2024, women age 40 and older died of maternal causes 3.8× as often as women age 25–39.
source_title: Hoyert, Donna L., "Maternal Mortality Rates in the United States, 2024," NCHS Health E-Stats
notes: The source group is "40 and older"; the site tag is age:40s. Women younger than 25: 13.7. Older age is also a medical risk factor, so this gap is not only about care quality.

statement: GPT-4 ranked résumés lower when they mentioned a disability, for example a disability-related award.
source_title: Glazko, Kate, et al., "Identifying and Improving Disability Bias in GPT-Based Resume Screening," FAccT 2024
notes: Audit study with GPT-4. The résumé with disability items was ranked first in only 15 of 60 trials (Table, the text says 15/70). A custom GPT trained on disability justice principles reduced the bias. The comparison résumé was identical except for the disability items (award, scholarship, talk or membership).

measure: photos classified as the right gender, average of 4 commercial face analysis services
statement: Face analysis tools labeled trans men as men about 7 in 10 times, and cisgender men almost every time.
source_title: Scheuerman, Morgan Klaus, Jacob M. Paul, and Jed R. Brubaker, "How Computers See Gender: An Evaluation of Gender Classification in Commercial Facial Analysis and Image Labeling Services," CSCW 2019
notes: Table 3 (PDF p. 14), text p. 15. 350 Instagram photos for each hashtag. The paper notes that it cannot know if the people in #man are cisgender.

measure: photos classified as the right gender, average of 4 commercial face analysis services
statement: Face analysis tools labeled trans women as women almost 9 in 10 times, and cisgender women almost every time.
source_title: Scheuerman, Morgan Klaus, Jacob M. Paul, and Jed R. Brubaker, "How Computers See Gender: An Evaluation of Gender Classification in Commercial Facial Analysis and Image Labeling Services," CSCW 2019
notes: Table 3 (PDF p. 14), text p. 15. 350 Instagram photos for each hashtag.

statement: Commercial face analysis tools can only label a face as male or female, so they can never classify a nonbinary person correctly.
source_title: Scheuerman, Morgan Klaus, Jacob M. Paul, and Jed R. Brubaker, "How Computers See Gender: An Evaluation of Gender Classification in Commercial Facial Analysis and Image Labeling Services," CSCW 2019
notes: The authors set the accuracy for #agender, #genderqueer and #nonbinary to 0% because no correct answer is possible (PDF p. 14). It is a missing category, not a measurement.

group: Deaf and hard of hearing speakers
measure: word error rate, average of 4 speech recognition systems (incl. OpenAI Whisper)
statement: Speech recognition systems made about 10× as many errors for deaf and hard of hearing speakers as for hearing speakers.
source_title: Zhao, Robin, Anna S.G. Choi, Allison Koenecke, and Anaïs Rameau, "Quantification of Automatic Speech Recognition System Performance on d/Deaf and Hard of Hearing Speech," The Laryngoscope
notes: Abstract and Table II. Small sample: 24 deaf or hard of hearing and 9 hearing speakers. Speakers who mainly use sign language: 70.2% errors; oral speakers only: 19.7%.

measure: word error rate, average of 5 speech recognition systems
statement: Speech recognition systems made about twice as many errors for Black men as for white men.
source_title: Koenecke, Allison, et al., "Racial Disparities in Automated Speech Recognition," PNAS
notes: Results section (0.41 vs 0.21). Systems tested in 2019.

measure: word error rate, average of 5 speech recognition systems
statement: Speech recognition systems made 1.8× as many errors for Black women as for white women.
source_title: Koenecke, Allison, et al., "Racial Disparities in Automated Speech Recognition," PNAS
notes: Results section (0.30 vs 0.17). Systems tested in 2019.

measure: language models choosing the death sentence in a hypothetical murder trial
statement: In a made-up murder case, language models chose the death sentence 1.2× as often when the defendant spoke African American English.
source_title: Hofmann, Valentin, Pratyusha Ria Kalluri, Dan Jurafsky, and Sharese King, "AI Generates Covertly Racist Decisions about People Based on Their Dialect," Nature
notes: Nature p. 150, Fig. 3c. The text said the same thing in two dialects; race was never named. Convictions: 68.7% vs 62.1%. Hypothetical decisions, not real courts.

measure: false matches per 100,000 comparisons, face recognition algorithm imperial_002
statement: One face recognition algorithm wrongly matched Vietnamese-born people about 50× as often as Polish-born people.
source_title: Grother, Patrick, Mei Ngan, and Kayee Hanaoka, "Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT) Part 3: Demographic Effects," NISTIR 8280
notes: PDF p. 34: false match rate 0.0024 (Vietnam) vs 0.000046 (Poland), same sex and country, any age. One algorithm only; country of birth is the report's proxy for race. NIST also found 2–5× more false matches for women than men, and the highest rates for people 65 and older.

measure: GPT-3.5 ranked the résumé first out of 8 equal résumés (financial analyst job)
statement: GPT-3.5 ranked a Black man's résumé first less often than an equally qualified white man's résumé.
source_title: Yin, Leon, Davey Alba, and Leonardo Nicoletti, "OpenAI's GPT Is a Recruiter's Dream Tool. Tests Show There's Racial Bias," Bloomberg (data on GitHub)
notes: From the authors' data file (performance ranking CSV). With no bias, each group would be first 12.5% of the time. One job and one model; results differ by job.

statement: Face recognition algorithms wrongly matched older people more often than middle-aged adults.
source_title: Grother, Patrick, Mei Ngan, and Kayee Hanaoka, "Face Recognition Vendor Test (FRVT) Part 3: Demographic Effects," NISTIR 8280
notes: PDF p. 5 and p. 54. The numbers are only in heatmap figures, so this is a finding. For women, people 65 and older had the highest false match rates.

measure: denial rate, all HMDA loan types and purposes (denied ÷ originated + approved-not-accepted + denied)
statement: In 2025, Black mortgage applicants were denied 1.8× as often as white applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, HMDA Data Browser (2025 Snapshot)
notes: Counts (originated / approved but not accepted / denied): Black 462,242 / 36,040 / 273,650; White 4,592,966 / 255,605 / 1,227,688. Denial rate = denied ÷ all three. "White" includes Hispanic white. All loan types (purchase, refinance, home equity), so rates are higher than for home purchase only. No controls for income, debt or credit. 2024: 36.7% vs 21.8%.

group: American Indian or Alaska Native applicants
measure: denial rate, all HMDA loan types and purposes
statement: In 2025, American Indian and Alaska Native mortgage applicants were denied 1.7× as often as white applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, HMDA Data Browser (2025 Snapshot)
notes: Counts (originated / approved but not accepted / denied): 40,526 / 3,539 / 23,653. Same data and limits as loan-black-denial-2025. 2024: 37.0%.

group: Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander applicants
measure: denial rate, all HMDA loan types and purposes
statement: In 2025, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander mortgage applicants were denied 1.7× as often as white applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, HMDA Data Browser (2025 Snapshot)
notes: Counts (originated / approved but not accepted / denied): 12,753 / 1,054 / 7,480. Small group (21,287 decisions). Same data and limits as loan-black-denial-2025. 2024: 38.7%.

measure: denial rate, all HMDA loan types and purposes
statement: In 2025, Asian mortgage applicants were denied about as often as white applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, HMDA Data Browser (2025 Snapshot)
notes: Counts (originated / approved but not accepted / denied): 411,030 / 23,628 / 112,039. Same data and limits as loan-black-denial-2025.

measure: denial rate, all HMDA loan types and purposes
statement: In 2025, Hispanic mortgage applicants were denied 1.4× as often as non-Hispanic applicants.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, HMDA Data Browser (2025 Snapshot)
notes: Counts (originated / approved but not accepted / denied): Hispanic 726,998 / 52,723 / 310,927; non-Hispanic 4,856,316 / 274,385 / 1,370,871. The comparison group is all non-Hispanic applicants (any race), not non-Hispanic white.

measure: denial rate, all HMDA loan types and purposes
statement: In 2025, women who applied for a mortgage alone were denied 1.1× as often as men who applied alone.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, HMDA Data Browser (2025 Snapshot)
notes: Counts (originated / approved but not accepted / denied): Female 1,406,812 / 93,974 / 564,020; Male 2,249,994 / 163,132 / 788,002. Joint applicants: 16.9%. HMDA records sex as male or female only.

statement: Black applicants were more likely to be denied a mortgage than white applicants, even with similar finances at the same lender.
source_title: García, Manu, and Carlos Garriga, "Determinants of Mortgage Denial," Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Review
notes: Abstract. Over 30 million home-purchase applications, HMDA 2018–2024, with lender and financial controls. Observable characteristics explain at most 41% of the gap. 7.8 percentage points more likely.

statement: Same-sex couples were 73% more likely to be denied a mortgage than different-sex couples.
source_title: Sun, Hua, and Lei Gao, "Lending Practices to Same-Sex Borrowers," PNAS
notes: HMDA 1990–2015; same-sex couples inferred from co-applicant sex. Old data, but the newest national study on LGBTQ+ mortgage access. They also paid higher fees, though they did not default more often.

statement: In 2026, women earned 83 cents for every dollar men earned.
source_title: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, "Usual Weekly Earnings of Wage and Salary Workers, Third Quarter 2026"
notes: Table 2, not seasonally adjusted. Released 2026-10-21. Annual 2025: $1,089 vs $1,326 (82.1%). The Census annual ratio is in paid-women-2025.

measure: unemployment rate (annual average)
statement: In 2025, people with a disability were unemployed twice as often as people without one.
source_title: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, "People with a Disability: Labor Force Characteristics — 2025"
notes: Table 1, 2025 annual averages (released 2026-03-03). The October 2025 survey was not collected, so 2025 is an 11-month average. Employment-population ratio: 22.8% vs 65.2%. 2023: 7.2% vs 3.5%.

measure: unemployment rate (annual average)
statement: In 2025, Black people with a disability were unemployed 1.6× as often as white people with a disability.
source_title: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, "People with a Disability: Labor Force Characteristics — 2025"
notes: Table 1. Hispanic: 9.5%, Asian: 7.9%. BLS race groups include Hispanic people of any race.

measure: unemployment rate (annual average)
statement: In 2025, Hispanic people with a disability were unemployed 1.3× as often as white people with a disability.
source_title: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, "People with a Disability: Labor Force Characteristics — 2025"
notes: Table 1. BLS race groups include Hispanic people of any race.

statement: At 108 of the largest US employers, applicants with Black-sounding names were contacted less often than applicants with white-sounding names.
source_title: Kline, Patrick, Evan K. Rose, and Christopher R. Walters, "Systemic Discrimination Among Large U.S. Employers," QJE
notes: Abstract. Data 2019–2021, published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2022. 83,000+ fake applications; Black-sounding names were contacted 2.1 percentage points less often. The gap was concentrated in a small set of firms.

statement: About 1 in 4 LGBTQ workers said they were not hired because they are LGBTQ.
source_title: Sears, Brad, et al., "LGBTQ People's Experiences of Workplace Discrimination and Harassment," Williams Institute, UCLA
notes: Key findings. Survey of 1,902 LGBTQ adults, summer 2023. Self-reported, not an audit. Lifetime discrimination or harassment at work: 47%; past year: 17%. Exact figures: 23% not hired, 21% fired because of sexual orientation or gender identity.

measure: share who ever experienced employment discrimination
statement: In 2023, trans and nonbinary workers reported discrimination at work 1.8× as often as cisgender LGBQ workers.
source_title: Sears, Brad, et al., "LGBTQ People's Experiences of Workplace Discrimination and Harassment," Williams Institute, UCLA
notes: Key findings. The source groups trans and nonbinary people together. The comparison group is cisgender LGBQ workers, not all workers. Past year: 22% vs 9%.

measure: share who ever experienced employment discrimination
statement: In 2023, LGBTQ people of color reported discrimination at work 1.6× as often as white LGBTQ people.
source_title: Sears, Brad, et al., "LGBTQ People's Experiences of Workplace Discrimination and Harassment," Williams Institute, UCLA
notes: Key findings. "People of color" is all non-white groups together (tag race:poc). Past year: 15% vs 7%.

statement: Newer AI models (2024 and later) did not favor white names over Black names when screening job applications.
source_title: Gao, Zhenyu, Wenxi Jiang, and Yutong Yan, "Can LLMs Hire Fairly? Racial Bias in Resume Screening," arXiv:2606.28978
notes: Abstract. Preprint (June 2026), not peer-reviewed yet. It tests newer models than the Bloomberg study. The same pattern held for gender. 14 models, 24,024 paired job postings each. The one 2023 model favored white names by 2.1 points; newer models showed no gap or favored Black names (up to 3.0 points).

statement: Women age 64–66 got fewer job callbacks than younger women.
source_title: Neumark, David, Ian Burn, and Patrick Button, "Is It Harder for Older Workers to Find Jobs? New and Improved Evidence from a Field Experiment," JPE
notes: Abstract. Data from 2015. Free version: NBER Working Paper 21669. 40,000+ applications, ages 64–66 vs 29–31. The study found much less evidence of age discrimination against older men.

measure: promotions to first-level manager per 100 men
statement: In 2025, 93 women were promoted to manager for every 100 men.
source_title: McKinsey & Company and LeanIn.Org, "Women in the Workplace 2025"
notes: Chart on p. 19 ("The broken rung persists"). Companies that share data have more women than average, so the real gap may be larger.

source_title: Fortune, Fortune 500 list (2026)
notes: Fortune contradicts itself: one June 3, 2026 article says 56 women CEOs (11.2%), another from the same day says 55 (11%). 2024: 10.4%.

group: American Indian and Alaska Native non-Hispanic people
measure: life expectancy at birth (years)
statement: In 2024, American Indian and Alaska Native people lived 7.8 fewer years on average than white people.
source_title: Arias, Elizabeth, et al., "United States Life Tables, 2024," National Vital Statistics Reports 75(5)
notes: Table A and the abstract. Published 2026-08-25. Life expectancy reflects more than health care. Total US: 79.0. In 2021 it was 65.2.

measure: life expectancy at birth (years)
statement: In 2024, Black people lived 4.1 fewer years on average than white people.
source_title: Arias, Elizabeth, et al., "United States Life Tables, 2024," National Vital Statistics Reports 75(5)
notes: Table A and the abstract. Published 2026-08-25. Life expectancy reflects more than health care. Hispanic: 81.8, Asian: 85.8.

statement: Only 4 in 10 US doctors were very confident they could give disabled patients the same quality of care.
source_title: Iezzoni, Lisa I., et al., "Physicians' Perceptions of People with Disability and Their Health Care," Health Affairs
notes: Abstract. Survey fielded 2019–2020; the newest national study of this kind. 714 doctors; 40.7% were very confident.

group: UCSD students with a Pell Grant
comparison_group: UCSD students with no Pell Grant or subsidized loan
measure: six-year graduation rate, first-time full-time students who started in fall 2019
statement: At UC San Diego, 81% of students with a Pell Grant graduated within six years, compared with 89% of students with no need-based aid.
source_title: UC San Diego Institutional Research, Common Data Set 2025–2026, section B
notes: Section B, fall 2019 cohort: Pell 1,536 of 1,895; neither 3,102 of 3,498; all students 86.0%. Year = the year the six years ended.

measure: four-year graduation rate, freshman entrants, University of California (all campuses)
statement: At the University of California, 66% of first-generation students graduated in four years, compared with 74% of all students.
source_title: University of California Information Center, Undergraduate graduation rates dashboard (Highlights)
notes: Highlights view, all UC campuses (not only UCSD). The dashboard does not name the cohort. The comparison group includes first-gen students. Pell: 67.9%.

statement: There is no official US pay data for nonbinary people: federal labor surveys record sex as male or female only.
source_title: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey
notes: Census Household Pulse asked about gender identity 2021–2025; in Feb 2025 Census moved to drop it (EO 14168). HMDA (loans) is also male/female only.

statement: There is no official US pay data by religion: federal surveys do not ask about religion.
source_title: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Current Population Survey
notes: Applies to all faith tags. Lenders also cannot ask about religion (ECOA / Regulation B).

statement: There is no national mortgage data by disability: HMDA does not record it.
source_title: FFIEC and CFPB, HMDA Data Browser
notes: No disability field in the HMDA LAR.

measure: callbacks for equally qualified applicants (meta-analysis of field experiments)
statement: Latino applicants got 81 callbacks for every 100 that equally qualified white applicants got.
source_title: Quillian, Lincoln, et al., "Meta-analysis of Field Experiments Shows No Change in Racial Discrimination in Hiring over Time," PNAS
notes: Results section (Abstract says the same). Random-effects meta-analysis of field experiments 1989–2015; 95% CI 15–33% more. Rates are written as 100 Latino callbacks for each 124 white callbacks. Published 2017. The authors found modest evidence that discrimination against Latinos declined over time; no change for Black applicants. 28 studies overall, 55,842 applications.

measure: callbacks for equally qualified applicants (meta-analysis of field experiments)
statement: Black applicants got 74 callbacks for every 100 that equally qualified white applicants got.
source_title: Quillian, Lincoln, et al., "Meta-analysis of Field Experiments Shows No Change in Racial Discrimination in Hiring over Time," PNAS
notes: Results section (Abstract says the same). Random-effects meta-analysis of field experiments 1989–2015; 95% CI 25–47% more. Rates are written as 100 Black callbacks for each 136 white callbacks. Published 2017. No change in the level of discrimination against Black applicants over 25 years.

measure: employer interest rate for accounting job applications (identical qualifications)
statement: Job applicants who mentioned a disability got 26% less interest from employers.
source_title: Ameri, Mason, et al., "The Disability Employment Puzzle: A Field Experiment on Employer Hiring Behavior," NBER Working Paper 21560
notes: p. 15 (text on Table 1, columns 1–2). 6,016 applications, June–August 2013; disabilities were spinal cord injury or Asperger's Syndrome, disclosed in the cover letter. Gap 1.71 points = 26% lower. Experienced applicants: 34% lower. Interview callbacks alone: 11% lower, not statistically significant. Published as ILR Review 2018.

measure: interview callback rate (paired résumés)
statement: Résumés that showed a man was gay got 37% fewer interview invitations.
source_title: Tilcsik, András, "Pride and Prejudice: Employment Discrimination against Openly Gay Men in the United States," American Journal of Sociology
notes: Table 5 and p. 22 of the author's preprint (https://osf.io/j9ybs). 1,769 job ads in 7 states, 2005; gay résumé listed a gay campus organization. Published 2011, AJS 117(2). Gap was large in Texas (12.0 vs 3.7) and Ohio (14.1 vs 5.5); not significant in CA, NV, NY, PA. Gap was bigger where no law banned sexual orientation discrimination (11.3 vs 5.3).

statement: Women who wore a hijab when they applied for jobs got fewer callbacks.
source_title: Ghumman, Sonia, and Ann Marie Ryan, "Not Welcome Here: Discrimination towards Women Who Wear the Muslim Headscarf," Human Relations
notes: Abstract (full text paywalled). Field experiment: confederates applied in person with or without a hijab. They also got less permission to complete applications, more negativity and less interest. Callbacks were lower where employees were less diverse. Year = publication year; data year not in abstract.

group: Applicants who listed a Muslim group
statement: In the American South, résumés that mentioned a Muslim group got among the fewest employer responses.
source_title: Wallace, Michael, Bradley R. E. Wright, and Allen Hyde, "Religious Affiliation and Hiring Discrimination in the American South: A Field Experiment," Social Currents
notes: Abstract (full text paywalled). Résumés were randomly changed to show one of seven religious groups or a control. Applicants with any religious identity were 26% less likely to get a response. Muslims, pagans and atheists faced the most discrimination; Jews faced none that could be seen. Year = publication year.

group: Applicants who listed an atheist group
statement: In the American South, résumés that mentioned an atheist group got among the fewest employer responses.
source_title: Wallace, Michael, Bradley R. E. Wright, and Allen Hyde, "Religious Affiliation and Hiring Discrimination in the American South: A Field Experiment," Social Currents
notes: Abstract (full text paywalled). Same study as hired-muslim-resume-south-finding. Muslims, pagans and atheists faced the most discrimination; Catholics moderate; evangelical Christians little; Jews none that could be seen. Year = publication year.

statement: Immigrants with the lightest skin earned about 17% more than similar immigrants with the darkest skin.
source_title: Hersch, Joni, "Immigrant Experience: The Relation between Skin Color and Pay," Communities & Banking (Federal Reserve Bank of Boston)
notes: Page 18, "Evidence" section. New Immigrant Survey 2003 (8,573 adults given green cards in 2003); interviewers rated skin color on a 0–10 scale. 17% controls for personal traits, pre-migration occupation, race, ethnicity and country of origin; it is 11% after also controlling for current job. Spring 2009 summary of Hersch, Journal of Labor Economics 26(2), 2008.

statement: About half of white medical students and residents believed a false idea about Black bodies, for example that Black people have thicker skin.
source_title: Hoffman, Kelly M., et al., "Racial Bias in Pain Assessment and Treatment Recommendations, and False Beliefs about Biological Differences between Blacks and Whites," PNAS
notes: Study 2 results and Table 1 (PMC4843483). 222 white medical students and residents; about 50% rated at least one false belief as possibly, probably or definitely true. Thicker skin item: 40% of first-years, 42% of second-years, 22% of third-years, 25% of residents; 58% of white laypeople (Study 1). Those with more false beliefs rated a Black patient's pain lower and gave less accurate treatment advice for him. Year = publication year; the paper gives no data-collection year.

statement: A widely used hospital algorithm rated Black patients as healthier than equally sick white patients, so fewer got extra care.
source_title: Obermeyer, Ziad, et al., "Dissecting Racial Bias in an Algorithm Used to Manage the Health of Populations," Science
notes: Abstract (PubMed 31649194). Fixing the bias would raise the share of Black patients picked for extra help from 17.7% to 46.5%. The bias comes from the algorithm predicting health care costs, not illness; less money is spent on Black patients. Year = publication year; full text (data years) is paywalled and was not checked.

statement: Bisexual women could not afford needed health care 1.6× as often as straight women.

notes: Table 6, p. 15. NHIS 2013–2018 pooled, adults 18+, adjusted for age and survey year. Six services: prescription medications, mental health counseling, dental care, eyeglasses, specialist care, follow-up care. Lesbian women: 24.7%. Both significantly different from heterosexual women. The report gives no combined LGB number. Read from the archived copy (cdc.gov blocks automated downloads).
